questions.question: In a fluid, the buoyant force acting on a submerged or floating object always acts _________.

options.text: in a direction depending on the shape of the object
along the direction of motion of the object

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**vertically upward**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Buoyancy** is the **upward force** exerted by a **fluid** (liquid or gas) that opposes the weight of a partially or fully immersed object. In any fluid, the pressure increases with depth; therefore, the fluid exerts more pressure on the bottom of an object than on the top, resulting in a net force acting **vertically upward**. ***Hence, option 1 is correct.***
 
• The direction of the **buoyant force** does not depend on the **shape** of the object but rather on the **gravity** field, which dictates that the net pressure difference will always push the object away from the center of gravity (upwards). ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The **weight** of the object acts **vertically downward** due to **gravity**. The buoyant force is the opposing force that pushes against this weight. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• The **buoyant force** acts independent of the **direction of motion** of the object. Whether an object is moving horizontally or vertically, the buoyant force remains directed **vertically upward** relative to the fluid's surface. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• The magnitude of this force is determined by **Archimedes' Principle**, which states that the upward buoyant force is equal to the **weight of the fluid** that the object **displaces**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Archimedes' Principle**: Discovered by the Greek mathematician **Archimedes** in the **3rd century BC**, this principle is fundamental to **fluid mechanics**. It explains why heavy **ships** made of **steel** can float while a small **iron nail** sinks.
 
• **Mathematical Formula**: The buoyant force (**Fb**) can be expressed as **Fb = ρ × V × g**, where **ρ (rho)** is the **density** of the fluid, **V** is the **volume** of the displaced fluid, and **g** is the **acceleration due to gravity** (approximately **9.8 m/s²**).
 
• **Factors Affecting Buoyancy**:
 
 
• **Density of the Fluid**: A higher fluid density results in a greater buoyant force. This is why it is easier to float in **saltwater** (like the **Dead Sea**) than in **freshwater**.
 
• **Volume of Displaced Fluid**: The more fluid an object displaces, the larger the upward force. Large **hulls** of ships are designed to displace massive amounts of water to support their weight.
 
 
 
• **Floating and Sinking**: 
 
 
• If the **buoyant force** is greater than the **weight** of the object, the object will **rise** to the surface and **float**.
 
• If the **weight** is greater than the buoyant force, the object will **sink**.
 
• If the **weight** equals the buoyant force, the object remains **neutrally buoyant** and stays suspended at its current depth.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Center of Buoyancy**: This is the point where the buoyant force is considered to act. It is the **geometric center** (centroid) of the **displaced volume** of fluid. For a floating object to be stable, the relationship between the **Center of Gravity** and the **Center of Buoyancy** is critical.
 
• **Apparent Weight**: When an object is submerged in water, it feels lighter. This "loss" in weight is called the **apparent weight**, which is the **actual weight** minus the **buoyant force**.
 
• **Applications**: The principle of buoyancy is used in the design of **submarines** (using **ballast tanks** to change density), **hot air balloons** (using heated air which is less dense than cool air), and **hydrometers** (used to measure the **specific gravity** of liquids).
</ul

questions.question: According to the sign convention for spherical mirrors, which option is correct about the focal length of a concave mirror?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Always negative**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to the **New Cartesian Sign Convention**, the **pole (P)** of the spherical mirror is taken as the **origin**, and the **principal axis** is taken as the **X-axis** of the coordinate system.
 
• A **concave mirror** is a **converging mirror** where the reflecting surface is curved inwards, towards the **center of curvature**.
 
• The **principal focus (F)** of a **concave mirror** is the point on the **principal axis** where rays of light parallel to the axis actually meet after reflection. This focus is situated in **front of the mirror**.
 
• Since the **object** is always placed on the **left side** of the mirror, the **incident light** travels from **left to right**. Distances measured in the **direction of incident light** are positive, while those measured **opposite to the direction of incident light** are negative.
 
• The **focal length (f)** is the distance between the **pole (P)** and the **principal focus (F)**. Because the focus of a **concave mirror** lies to the **left of the pole**, this distance is measured against the direction of incident light. ***Hence, the focal length of a concave mirror is always negative.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **New Cartesian Sign Convention Rules:**
 
 
• The **object** is always placed to the **left** of the mirror. This implies that the **object distance (u)** is always **negative**.
 
• All distances parallel to the **principal axis** are measured from the **pole** of the mirror.
 
• Distances measured to the **right of the origin** (+x-axis) are **positive**, and those to the **left** (-x-axis) are **negative**.
 
• Distances measured **perpendicularly above** the principal axis (+y-axis) are **positive**, and those **below** (-y-axis) are **negative**.
 
 
 
• **Convex Mirror:**
 
 
• A **convex mirror** is a **diverging mirror** with its reflecting surface curved outwards.
 
• Its **principal focus** is a **virtual point** located **behind the mirror** (on the right side).
 
• Therefore, the **focal length (f)** of a **convex mirror** is **always positive**.
 
 
 
• **Mirror Formula and Magnification:**
 
 
• The **mirror formula** represents the relationship between **focal length (f)**, **object distance (u)**, and **image distance (v)**: **1/f = 1/v + 1/u**.
 
• **Magnification (m)** is the ratio of the **height of the image (h')** to the **height of the object (h)**, also expressed as **m = -v/u**.
 
• For a **concave mirror**, the **radius of curvature (R)** is also **negative**, and the relationship is **R = 2f**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Concave Mirrors:**
 
 
• They are used in **shaving mirrors** and **makeup mirrors** to produce an **enlarged and erect image** when the object is held close.
 
• They are used as **reflectors** in **car headlights**, **searchlights**, and **torches** to produce a **powerful parallel beam** of light.
 
• **Solar furnaces** use large **concave mirrors** to **concentrate sunlight** to produce high temperatures for melting metals.
 
• **Dentists** use them to see **larger images** of the teeth of patients.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **focal length** of a **plane mirror** is considered to be **infinity** because the **radius of curvature** of a flat surface is infinite.
 
• The **sign of the image distance (v)** in a **concave mirror** can be **positive or negative** depending on the position of the object. If the image is **real** (formed in front), **v is negative**; if the image is **virtual** (formed behind), **v is positive**.
 
• The **focal length** of a spherical mirror depends only on its **radius of curvature** and is **independent** of the **medium** in which it is placed (unlike lenses).
</ul

questions.question: Which statement best defines the term 'formula unit mass' as used in the context of ionic compounds?

options.text: It is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms present in a formula unit of an ionic compound.
It is the product of the atomic masses of all elements in a compound.
It is the total number of atoms in a molecule of a covalent compound.
It is the mass of one mole of a molecular compound.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms present in a formula unit of an ionic compound**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **formula unit mass** of a substance is defined as the **sum of the atomic masses** of all atoms in a **formula unit** of a compound. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• It is calculated in the same manner as **molecular mass**; however, the term "formula unit" is specifically used for substances whose constituent particles are **ions** (ionic compounds) rather than discrete molecules.
 
• Statement 2 suggests it is the **product** of atomic masses, which is scientifically incorrect as masses are always additive in this context to determine the total mass of a unit. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• Statement 3 refers to the **total number of atoms** in a molecule, which is actually the definition of **atomicity** (e.g., O2 has an atomicity of 2). ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• Statement 4 describes the **mass of one mole** of a compound, which is known as the **molar mass**, typically expressed in **grams per mole (g/mol)**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• The unit used for expressing formula unit mass is the **atomic mass unit**, represented by the symbol **‘u’** (unified mass).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ionic Compounds vs. Molecular Compounds**:
 
 
• In **molecular compounds** (like **water, H2O**), atoms are bonded **covalently** to form distinct molecules. We use the term **molecular mass** here.
 
• In **ionic compounds** (like **Sodium Chloride, NaCl**), the structure consists of a **three-dimensional crystal lattice** of alternating **cations** and **anions**. Since there are no individual "NaCl molecules," we use the **formula unit** (the simplest whole-number ratio of ions) to calculate mass.
 
 
 
• **Calculation Example (Sodium Chloride)**:
 
 
• The formula unit of sodium chloride is **NaCl**.
 
• **Atomic mass of Sodium (Na)** = **23 u**.
 
• **Atomic mass of Chlorine (Cl)** = **35.5 u**.
 
• **Formula unit mass** = **1 × 23 + 1 × 35.5** = **58.5 u**.
 
 
 
• **Calculation Example (Calcium Chloride)**:
 
 
• The formula unit is **CaCl2**.
 
• **Atomic mass of Calcium (Ca)** = **40 u**.
 
• **Atomic mass of Chlorine (Cl)** = **35.5 u**.
 
• **Formula unit mass** = **40 + (2 × 35.5)** = **40 + 71** = **111 u**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Relative Atomic Mass**: All these calculations are based on the **relative atomic mass** of elements, which is determined relative to the **Carbon-12 (12C)** isotope, where 1 u is **1/12th the mass** of one atom of carbon-12.
 
• **Significance in Stoichiometry**: Understanding formula unit mass is crucial for **quantitative chemistry** and **stoichiometry**, allowing scientists to calculate the exact amount of **reactants** and **products** in a chemical reaction involving ionic substances.
 
• **Molar Mass Connection**: If the formula unit mass of **NaCl** is **58.5 u**, then its **molar mass** is numerically the same but expressed in grams, i.e., **58.5 g**, which contains **6.022 × 10^23** (Avogadro's number) formula units.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of work done?

options.text: Pulling a trolley along a flat surface
Lifting a brick from the floor

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pushing a wall**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In physics, **Work** is defined as the product of the **Force** applied to an object and the **Displacement** caused by that force in the direction of the force.
 
• The mathematical formula for work done is **W = F × s × cos(θ)**, where **W** is work, **F** is the magnitude of force, **s** is the displacement, and **θ** is the angle between the force and displacement vectors.
 
• For work to be considered "done" in a scientific sense, two conditions must be met: a **force** must act on the object, and the object must possess a **non-zero displacement**.
 
• **Pulling a trolley along a flat surface**: In this case, a force is applied and the trolley moves a certain distance. Since there is displacement, work is done. ***Hence, statement 1 is an example of work.***
 
• **Lifting a brick from the floor**: A force is applied upwards to overcome **gravity**, and the brick moves from the floor to a height. Since displacement occurs in the direction of the force, work is done. ***Hence, statement 2 is an example of work.***
 
• **Pushing a wall**: When a person pushes a rigid wall, they apply a significant amount of **force**. However, because the wall does not move, the **displacement (s) is 0**. According to the formula, if **s = 0**, then **W = 0**. ***Hence, statement 3 is NOT an example of work done.***
 
• **Sliding luggage on the floor**: Force is applied to overcome **friction**, and the luggage moves across the floor. Since displacement occurs, work is performed. ***Hence, statement 4 is an example of work.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Nature of Work**: 
 
 
• **Positive Work**: When the force and displacement are in the **same direction** (angle **θ = 0°**), the work done is positive.
 
• **Negative Work**: When the force and displacement are in **opposite directions** (angle **θ = 180°**), such as the force of **friction** acting on a moving body, the work done is negative.
 
• **Zero Work**: This occurs when displacement is zero or when the force is **perpendicular** to the displacement (angle **θ = 90°**). A classic example is a **coolie** carrying a load on his head while walking horizontally; the force of gravity is downward, but displacement is horizontal.
 
 
 
• **Units and Measurements**:
 
 
• The **S.I. unit** of work is the **Joule (J)**. **One Joule** is defined as the work done when a force of **1 Newton** displaces an object by **1 meter**.
 
• In the **CGS system**, the unit of work is the **erg**. **1 Joule** is equal to **10⁷ ergs**.
 
• Work is a **scalar quantity**, meaning it has only magnitude and no direction.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Work-Energy Theorem**: It states that the **net work done** on an object is equal to the change in its **Kinetic Energy**. This establishes a direct link between motion and the effort exerted.
 
• **Dimensional Formula**: The dimensional representation of work is **[M1 L2 T-2]**, which is the same as that of **energy** and **torque**.
 
• **Power**: While work represents the total energy transferred, **Power** is the **rate** at which work is done. It is measured in **Watts (W)**, where **1 Watt = 1 Joule per second**.
 
• **Conservative Forces**: Work done by **gravitational** or **electrostatic forces** depends only on the initial and final positions, not on the path taken. These are known as **conservative forces**.

questions.question: Evaporation takes place at which temperature?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**At any temperature**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Evaporation** is a fundamental physical process where a liquid changes into its vapor state at the **surface**. This process occurs at **any temperature** below the boiling point of the liquid.
 
• It is classified as a **surface phenomenon** because it only involves the molecules located at the top layer of the liquid, unlike boiling which affects the entire volume.
 
• Molecules in a liquid are in constant motion and possess different levels of **kinetic energy**. At **any temperature**, a small fraction of molecules at the surface has enough energy to overcome the **intermolecular forces** of attraction and escape into the air as gas.
 
• Since the molecules with the highest energy escape, the average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid decreases, which leads to a **cooling effect**.
 
• The process of evaporation is continuous and happens even at very low temperatures, though the rate may be significantly slower compared to higher temperatures. ***Hence, the correct answer is At any temperature.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Factors Affecting the Rate of Evaporation:**
 
 
• **Temperature:** As the **temperature** increases, more molecules gain enough **kinetic energy** to convert into vapor, thereby increasing the rate of evaporation.
 
• **Surface Area:** Since evaporation is a **surface phenomenon**, increasing the **exposed surface area** (e.g., spreading out wet clothes) allows more molecules to escape simultaneously.
 
• **Humidity:** The rate of evaporation is inversely proportional to **humidity**. If the air is already saturated with water vapor, the liquid evaporates more slowly.
 
• **Wind Speed:** An increase in **wind speed** helps move the vapor particles away from the surface, making room for more molecules to evaporate.
 
 
 
• **Evaporation vs. Boiling:**
 
 
• **Boiling** occurs only at a specific temperature called the **boiling point** (which is **100 degrees Celsius** for pure water at sea level).
 
• **Boiling** is a **bulk phenomenon** where bubbles form throughout the liquid, whereas evaporation is limited to the surface.
 
• While evaporation happens at **all temperatures**, boiling requires a constant supply of **external heat** to maintain the temperature at the boiling point.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Latent Heat of Vaporization:** This is the amount of **heat energy** required to change **1 kilogram** of a liquid into gas at its boiling point without a change in temperature. During evaporation, the liquid absorbs this "latent heat" from the surroundings, resulting in the characteristic **cooling effect**.
 
• **Real-world Applications:**
 
 
• **Earthen Pots (Matkas):** Water stays cool in earthen pots because water evaporates through the **pores** of the pot, taking heat from the water inside.
 
• **Sweating:** The human body uses evaporation to regulate **internal temperature**. As **sweat** evaporates from the skin, it absorbs body heat, providing a cooling sensation.
 
• **Acetone/Perfume:** When you put **acetone** or **perfume** on your palm, it evaporates rapidly because of its low boiling point, making your palm feel very cold.
 
 
 
• **Vapor Pressure:** Evaporation continues until the **vapor pressure** above the liquid reaches a state of **equilibrium** with the liquid itself in a closed container. In an open system, it can continue until the liquid is completely gone.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following metals can be shaped into leaves by pressure of the fingers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sodium**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sodium** is a member of the **alkali metal** group, located in **Group 1** of the periodic table with the symbol **Na** and **Atomic Number 11**.
 
• One of the most distinctive physical properties of **Sodium** is its extreme **softness**; it has a consistency similar to soft **wax** or **clay** at room temperature.
 
• Unlike most common metals such as **Iron** or **Copper**, **Sodium** is so soft that it can be easily sliced with a **stainless steel knife**.
 
• Because of this low **structural hardness** and **tensile strength**, **Sodium** can be flattened or shaped into thin **leaves** or sheets simply by applying the **pressure of the fingers**.
 
• This property is a result of the **metallic bonding** in **alkali metals**, which involves only **one valence electron**, leading to a relatively weak lattice structure compared to **transition metals**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Reactivity and Storage**:
 
 
• **Sodium** is highly **reactive**, especially with **water** and **oxygen**. To prevent it from reacting with moisture in the **atmosphere**, it is strictly stored under **kerosene oil** or **liquid paraffin**.
 
• When it reacts with **water**, it produces **sodium hydroxide** and **hydrogen gas**, often resulting in a vigorous or explosive reaction.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Options**:
 
 
• **Gold (Au)**: It is the most **malleable** and **ductile** metal known. While it can be beaten into incredibly thin **gold leaves** (foils), this process requires mechanical hammering or rolling; it cannot be shaped from a solid block into a leaf by mere **finger pressure** due to its higher **density** and **atomic weight**.
 
• **Silver (Ag)**: Similar to gold, **silver** is highly **malleable** and used for making fine foils (like **Chandi ka Varq** used in sweets), but it possesses a crystalline structure that is much firmer than **Sodium**.
 
• **Iron (Fe)**: A **transition metal** known for its **strength** and **hardness**. It has a high **melting point** of **1538°C** and requires heavy machinery or high temperatures (forging) to be shaped.
 
 
 
• **Physical Constants of Sodium**:
 
 
• The **melting point** of **Sodium** is relatively low at approximately **97.8°C**.
 
• Its **density** is **0.97 g/cm³**, which is less than that of **water**, meaning it will float while reacting.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Electronic Configuration**: **Sodium** has an electronic configuration of **[Ne] 3s¹**. The presence of a single **outer shell electron** makes it highly likely to lose that electron to achieve a stable **octet**, forming the **Na+ cation**.
 
• **Flame Test**: When **Sodium** or its salts are introduced to a **Bunsen burner flame**, they impart a characteristic **persistent golden-yellow color**, which is a standard qualitative analysis test.
 
• **Natural Occurrence**: Due to its extreme **reactivity**, **Sodium** is never found in its **elemental state** in nature. It is primarily obtained through the **electrolysis** of **molten sodium chloride** (Downs process).
</ul

questions.question: What is the geometric relationship between the principal axis and the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror at the point of the pole P?

options.text: The principal axis is parallel to the mirror surface.
The principal axis intersects the mirror at an oblique angle.
The principal axis is normal (perpendicular) to the mirror at its pole.
The principal axis is tangent to the mirror surface.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The principal axis is normal (perpendicular) to the mirror at its pole**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Principal Axis** of a spherical mirror is an imaginary straight line that passes through the **Center of Curvature (C)** and the **Pole (P)** of the mirror.
 
• A spherical mirror (whether **Concave** or **Convex**) is a segment of a **Hollow Sphere**. According to the laws of geometry, any line drawn from the center of a sphere to its surface is a **Radius**.
 
• A **Radius** is always **Normal (Perpendicular)** to the surface of the sphere at the point where it intersects. Since the **Principal Axis** passes through the **Center of Curvature**, it acts as a normal to the mirror’s surface at the **Pole (P)**. ***Hence, the statement regarding its perpendicularity is correct.***
 
• This geometric relationship ensures that a ray of light traveling along the **Principal Axis** strikes the mirror at an **Angle of Incidence** of **0 degrees** relative to the normal, causing it to reflect back along the same path.
 
• At the **Pole**, the **Principal Axis** is at an angle of **90 degrees** to the **Tangent** drawn at the pole on the mirror's reflecting surface.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Components of a Spherical Mirror:**
 
 
• **Pole (P)**: This is the **Geometric Center** of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror. It is located exactly on the surface of the mirror.
 
• **Center of Curvature (C)**: It is the center of the **Hollow Glass Sphere** of which the mirror is a part. For a **Concave Mirror**, it lies in front of the reflecting surface, whereas for a **Convex Mirror**, it lies behind it.
 
• **Radius of Curvature (R)**: This is the linear distance between the **Pole** and the **Center of Curvature (PC)**. It represents the radius of the sphere from which the mirror was cut.
 
• **Principal Focus (F)**: It is a point on the **Principal Axis** where light rays that are parallel to the axis converge (in **Concave Mirrors**) or appear to diverge from (in **Convex Mirrors**) after reflection.
 
• **Focal Length (f)**: The distance between the **Pole** and the **Principal Focus** is known as the **Focal Length**. For mirrors with a small **Aperture**, the relationship is **R = 2f**.
 
 
 
• **Types of Spherical Mirrors:**
 
 
• **Concave Mirror**: Also known as a **Converging Mirror**, its reflecting surface is curved inwards. It is used in **Headlights**, **Solar Furnaces**, and by **Dentists** to see enlarged images.
 
• **Convex Mirror**: Also known as a **Diverging Mirror**, its reflecting surface is curved outwards. It always forms a **Virtual, Erect, and Diminished** image and is primarily used as **Rear-view Mirrors** in vehicles because of its wide field of view.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Sign Convention (New Cartesian Sign Convention):**
 
 
• The **Pole (P)** is taken as the **Origin**.
 
• Objects are always placed to the **Left** of the mirror.
 
• Distances measured in the direction of **Incident Light** (to the right) are taken as **Positive**, while those measured against it (to the left) are **Negative**.
 
• The **Focal Length** of a **Concave Mirror** is always **Negative**, and for a **Convex Mirror**, it is always **Positive**.
 
 
 
• **Aperture:** The diameter of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror is called its **Aperture**. In most educational problems, we assume the **Aperture** is much smaller than the **Radius of Curvature**.
</ul

questions.question: Corrosion causes damage to the metal body, especially:

options.text: in both dry air and oil

questions.solution:
p-The correct answer is __**in moist air**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Corrosion** is a natural process that converts a refined metal into a more chemically stable form such as oxide, hydroxide, or sulfide. It is an **electrochemical process** that gradually destroys materials through chemical reactions with their environment.
 
• The presence of **moist air**, which contains both **oxygen** and **water vapor**, is the essential condition for the **rusting** of iron and the corrosion of many other metals. Water acts as an **electrolyte**, allowing the flow of ions between the **anodic** and **cathodic** regions on the metal surface. ***Hence, the statement "in moist air" is correct.***
 
• In **dry air**, the lack of moisture prevents the formation of an electrolytic medium. Without water, the movement of ions is restricted, and the **oxidation** of the metal happens extremely slowly or not at all at **room temperature**. ***Hence, the statement "in dry air" is incorrect.***
 
• **Galvanisation** is actually a **protective measure** against corrosion. It involves coating iron or steel with a thin layer of **zinc** to prevent oxygen and moisture from reaching the underlying metal. ***Hence, the statement "by galvanisation" is incorrect as it prevents rather than causes damage.***
 
• The presence of **oil** acts as a barrier that seals the metal surface from the atmosphere. By excluding both **oxygen** and **moisture**, oil prevents the chemical reaction required for corrosion to occur. ***Hence, the statement "in both dry air and oil" is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Rusting of Iron:** This is the most common form of corrosion. The chemical formula for rust is **Fe2O3 · xH2O** (hydrated iron(III) oxide). It occurs when iron reacts with oxygen in the presence of water. Unlike some other metal oxides, rust is **porous** and flakes off, exposing fresh metal to further corrosion.
 
• **Corrosion of Copper:** When exposed to moist air, **copper** develops a green coating. This green substance is a mixture of **copper hydroxide** and **copper carbonate**, often referred to as **patina**.
 
• **Tarnishing of Silver:** Silver objects turn black when exposed to air containing **hydrogen sulfide gas**. The black coating is **silver sulfide (Ag2S)**, which is a result of a chemical reaction with sulfur compounds in the **atmosphere**.
 
• **Factors Accelerating Corrosion:** The rate of corrosion increases in the presence of **impurities** in the metal, high **temperature**, and electrolytes like **saltwater**. This is why ships and structures in **coastal areas** corrode much faster than those in inland regions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Prevention Methods:** To save metals from damage, several techniques are used, including **painting**, **oiling**, **greasing**, **electroplating**, and **alloying**. 
 
• **Alloying:** Creating an alloy such as **stainless steel** (a mixture of iron, **carbon**, **chromium**, and **nickel**) makes the metal highly resistant to corrosion because the chromium forms a thin, invisible layer of **chromium oxide** on the surface.
 
• **Economic Impact:** Every **year**, corrosion causes significant damage to **car bodies**, **bridges**, **iron railings**, and **ships**, leading to massive financial losses in the global **industrial sector**.
 
• **Sacrificial Protection:** In this method, a more **reactive metal** (like **magnesium** or **zinc**) is attached to the metal to be protected. The more reactive metal corrodes first, "sacrificing" itself to protect the primary structure.

questions.question: In mitosis, how do the chromosomes in daughter cells compare with those in the parent cell?

options.text: Daughter cells lose all chromosomes during division.
Daughter cells contain twice the number of chromosomes as the parent cell.
Daughter cells have the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell.
Daughter cells have half the number of chromosomes as the parent cell.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Daughter cells have the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mitosis** is a fundamental process of **cell division** where a single **parent cell** divides to produce **two genetically identical daughter cells**.
 
• The primary function of mitosis is the **growth** of the organism and the **repair or replacement** of damaged tissues.
 
• During the **S phase** of **Interphase** (the phase preceding mitosis), the cell replicates its **DNA**. This ensures that there is a duplicate copy of every **chromosome** available for the division process.
 
• Because the genetic material is duplicated and then partitioned equally, the **daughter cells** maintain the exact same **chromosomal number** as the original parent cell.
 
• In biological terms, if the parent cell is **diploid (2n)**, the resulting daughter cells will also be **diploid (2n)**. ***Hence, the statement that daughter cells have the same number of chromosomes is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Stages of Mitosis:** Mitosis is a continuous process but is generally divided into **four main stages**:
 
 
• **Prophase:** The **chromatin** condenses into visible **chromosomes**, and the **nuclear envelope** begins to disappear.
 
• **Metaphase:** The **chromosomes** align along the **equatorial plane** (metaphase plate) of the cell, ensuring proper separation.
 
• **Anaphase:** The **sister chromatids** are pulled apart by **spindle fibers** toward opposite **poles** of the cell.
 
• **Telophase:** New **nuclear membranes** form around the two sets of separated chromosomes, which begin to de-condense back into chromatin.
 
 
 
• **Equational Division:** Mitosis is often referred to as **equational division** because the number of chromosomes remains constant from the parent to the daughter cells.
 
• **Comparison with Meiosis:** Unlike mitosis, **meiosis** is a "reduction division" occurring in **germ cells** to produce **gametes** (sperm and eggs). In meiosis, the daughter cells end up with **half (haploid, n)** the number of chromosomes compared to the parent cell.
 
• **Cytokinesis:** This is the final step of the cell cycle where the **cytoplasm** of the parent cell physically divides into two, resulting in two distinct **daughter cells**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Chromosome Count in Humans:** In a typical human **somatic cell**, there are **46 chromosomes** (**23 pairs**). After undergoing **mitosis**, each of the **two daughter cells** will also contain **46 chromosomes**.
 
• **Genetic Stability:** Mitosis is crucial for maintaining **genomic integrity**. By producing **clones** of the parent cell, it ensures that every cell in a multicellular organism (except gametes) carries the same **genetic information**.
 
• **Occurrence:** In humans and many animals, mitosis occurs almost everywhere in the body, such as the **skin**, **bone marrow**, and **lining of the gut**, where constant cell turnover is required.
 
• **Discovery:** The process of mitosis was first observed and described by the German biologist **Walther Flemming** in the year **1882**.
</ul

questions.question: What is the term used for the division of cytoplasm following nuclear division?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cytokinesis**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cytokinesis** is the physical process of **cell division**, which divides the **cytoplasm** of a parental cell into two daughter cells.
 
• It typically begins during the late stages of nuclear division (**Anaphase** or **Telophase**) and ensures that each daughter cell receives a nucleus and a share of **cytoplasmic organelles**.
 
• In **animal cells**, the process occurs through the formation of a **cleavage furrow**. A **contractile ring** composed of **actin** and **myosin** filaments constricts the cell membrane inward until the cell is pinched into two.
 
• In **plant cells**, due to the presence of a rigid **cell wall**, a cleavage furrow cannot form. Instead, a **cell plate** is synthesized in the center of the cell by the fusion of **Golgi-derived vesicles**, which then grows outward to join the existing lateral walls.
 
• This stage marks the completion of the **M phase** (Mitotic phase) of the **cell cycle**, resulting in two distinct cells that can then enter the **G1 phase** of **Interphase**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Karyokinesis**:
 
 
• This refers to the division of the **cell nucleus** during mitosis or meiosis. It is divided into four main stages: **Prophase**, **Metaphase**, **Anaphase**, and **Telophase**.
 
• While **cytokinesis** deals with the cytoplasm, **karyokinesis** ensures the equal distribution of replicated **DNA** (chromosomes) into the daughter nuclei.
 
 
 
• **Interphase**:
 
 
• Known as the preparatory phase, it accounts for approximately **95%** of the duration of the **cell cycle**.
 
• It is divided into three sub-phases: **G1** (cell growth), **S** (DNA replication), and **G2** (further growth and protein synthesis). During the **S phase**, the amount of **DNA** per cell doubles, but the **chromosome number** remains the same.
 
 
 
• **Chromatin Condensation**:
 
 
• This process occurs primarily during **Prophase**. The diffuse network of **DNA** and proteins (**chromatin**) undergoes coiling and folding to form compact, visible **chromosomes**.
 
• Condensation is crucial for the safe transport of genetic material to the opposite poles of the cell without entanglement or breakage.
 
 
 
• **Syncytium**:
 
 
• In some organisms, **karyokinesis** is not followed by **cytokinesis**, leading to a multinucleate condition.
 
• A classic biological example is the **liquid endosperm** in **coconut**, where many nuclei exist within a common cytoplasm before cellularization occurs.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The term **mitosis** is often used interchangeably with the **M phase**, but technically, mitosis refers to **karyokinesis** (nuclear division), while the total cell splitting is only complete after **cytokinesis**.
 
• The **centrosomes** and **spindle fibers** play a vital role in **karyokinesis** by pulling **sister chromatids** apart during **Anaphase**.
 
• Errors in **cytokinesis** or **karyokinesis** can lead to **aneuploidy** (abnormal number of chromosomes) or **polyploidy**, which are often linked to **cancer** development or specific evolutionary traits in plants.
 
• The regulatory proteins called **cyclins** and **cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs)** control the transition between these various stages of the **cell cycle** to ensure genomic stability.
</ul

the Western Ghats and Eastern Himalayas

questions.question: If a fertilised egg reaches the uterus but finds the lining thin and not spongy, what could happen?

options.text: The egg survives longer than usual.
Menstruation is delayed but still occurs.
The embryo fails to implant properly and is expelled.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The embryo fails to implant properly and is expelled**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Uterus** (womb) is a major female hormone-responsive secondary sex organ. Each month, the inner lining of the uterus, known as the **Endometrium**, prepares itself to receive a **Fertilised Egg**.
 
• For a successful pregnancy, the **Endometrium** must become **Thick** and **Spongy**, enriched with **Blood Vessels** and nutrients to support the **Embryo**.
 
• **Implantation** is the process where the **Blastocyst** (the early-stage embryo) attaches to the uterine wall. If the lining is **Thin** and not spongy, the embryo cannot find a secure place to anchor or receive nourishment. ***Hence, the statement that the embryo fails to implant properly and is expelled is correct.***
 
• If the **Fertilised Egg** (embryo) fails to implant, the body does not receive the hormonal signal (**HCG**) to maintain the thickened lining. Consequently, the lining breaks down, and the embryo is shed along with the blood and tissues during **Menstruation**.
 
• The idea that the egg survives longer than usual is biologically incorrect, as a non-implanted embryo has a very limited window of viability without maternal support. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• The claim that the egg gets fertilised again is impossible because **Fertilisation** occurs in the **Fallopian Tube**, and once an egg is fertilised, the **Zona Pellucida** hardens to prevent **Polyspermy**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Role of Progesterone:** This hormone is primarily responsible for making the **Endometrium** "spongy" and **Secretory**. It is produced by the **Corpus Luteum** after **Ovulation**. If **Progesterone** levels are low, the lining remains thin, leading to **Infertility**.
 
• **The Menstrual Cycle:** It consists of several phases. During the **Proliferative Phase**, **Estrogen** causes the lining to thicken. During the **Secretory Phase**, the lining becomes prepared for **Implantation**. If no implantation occurs, the **Menstrual Phase** begins.
 
• **Fertilisation vs. Implantation:** **Fertilisation** is the union of **Sperm** and **Ovum**, typically occurring in the **Ampulla** of the **Fallopian Tube**. **Implantation** occurs about **6 to 10 days** later in the **Uterus**.
 
• **Endometrial Thickness:** In clinical medicine, a thickness of at least **7 mm** to **8 mm** is usually considered necessary for a high chance of successful **Embryo Implantation** during **IVF** or natural cycles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (HCG):** This is the "pregnancy hormone." It is produced by the cells surrounding a growing embryo, which eventually form the **Placenta**. Its primary role is to keep the **Corpus Luteum** producing **Progesterone**, preventing the **Menstrual Cycle** from starting.
 
• **Luteal Phase Deficiency:** This is a condition where the **Uterine Lining** does not develop sufficiently because of inadequate **Progesterone** levels or the lining's failure to respond to the hormone, often leading to **Early Miscarriage**.
 
• **Expulsion Process:** When implantation fails, the embryo, which is microscopic at this stage, is expelled naturally. This often goes unnoticed as it occurs around the same time as a regular **Menstrual Period**.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of the third law of motion?

options.text: A rocket moving upward due to gases expelled downward.
Foot pushes the ground backward and ground pushes the foot forward.
The swimmer pushes the water backward with her hands.
Pushing a stationary car and making it move.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pushing a stationary car and making it move**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Newton's Third Law of Motion** states that for every **action**, there is an **equal and opposite reaction**. This means that forces always exist in pairs, and the two forces act on **different bodies** simultaneously.
 
• **A rocket moving upward due to gases expelled downward**: This is a classic example of the **third law**. The rocket engine expels hot exhaust gases **downward** (action), and these gases exert an equal force on the rocket **upward** (reaction). ***Hence, this is an example of the third law.***
 
• **Foot pushes the ground backward and ground pushes the foot forward**: When we walk, our feet exert a **backward force** on the ground (action). According to the law, the ground exerts an equal and **forward force** on our feet (reaction), allowing us to move. ***Hence, this is an example of the third law.***
 
• **The swimmer pushes the water backward with her hands**: A swimmer exerts a force on the water in the **backward direction** (action). In response, the water exerts an **equal force** on the swimmer in the **forward direction** (reaction), pushing her through the water. ***Hence, this is an example of the third law.***
 
• **Pushing a stationary car and making it move**: While there is a reaction force on the person's hands, the act of changing the state of a stationary object involves **overcoming inertia** and applying an **unbalanced force** to create **acceleration**. This is primarily described by **Newton's Second Law** (**F = ma**) and the **First Law** (Law of Inertia). ***Hence, this is NOT a primary example of the third law in this context.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Newton's First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia):** It states that an object will remain at **rest** or move in a **straight line** at a **constant velocity** unless acted upon by an **external unbalanced force**. The tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion is called **Inertia**, which depends on the **mass** of the object.
 
• **Newton's Second Law of Motion:** This law defines force quantitatively. It states that the **rate of change of momentum** of an object is directly proportional to the applied **force** and takes place in the direction of the force. The mathematical formula is **Force (F) = mass (m) × acceleration (a)**.
 
• **Sir Isaac Newton:** He was an English mathematician and physicist who formulated the three laws of motion in his work **"Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica"**, published in **1687**. These laws form the foundation of **classical mechanics**.
 
• **Conservation of Momentum:** Newton's Third Law leads to the principle of **conservation of linear momentum**. In an isolated system where no external forces act, the **total momentum** remains **constant** over time, regardless of internal changes or collisions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Force Pairs:** It is important to note that the **action and reaction** forces never act on the **same body**. If they did, the **net force** on every object would always be **zero**, and motion would be impossible.
 
• **Simultaneity:** There is no **time lag** between action and reaction; they occur at the exact same **instant**.
 
• **Magnitude and Direction:** The two forces in a third-law pair always have the **same magnitude** but act in exactly **opposite directions**.
 
• **Applications in Technology:** The third law is essential for the design of **jet engines**, **propellers**, **recoil mechanisms in guns**, and even the simple act of **rowing a boat**.

questions.question: In daily life, the principle of force on a current-carrying conductor is used in which of the following devices?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Electric motor**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Electric motor** is a rotating device that converts **electrical energy** into **mechanical energy**. It is based on the principle that a **current-carrying conductor** placed in a **magnetic field** experiences a **mechanical force**.
 
• When a **rectangular coil** carrying current is placed in a magnetic field, the **magnetic force** acts on the arms of the coil, causing it to rotate continuously. ***Hence, the correct answer is Electric motor.***
 
• **Electric fuse**: It is a safety device used in electrical circuits that works on the **heating effect of electric current** (Joule heating). It consists of a wire with a **low melting point** that melts and breaks the circuit if the **current** exceeds a safe limit. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• **Electric heater**: This device converts **electrical energy** into **heat energy** using a high-resistance heating element, typically made of **Nichrome**. It operates purely on the **thermal effect** of current rather than mechanical force. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Electric bell**: While it uses **electromagnetism**, its operation relies on the **magnetic effect of electric current** to attract an armature (striker) periodically. It does not use the continuous **force on a conductor** in the same way a motor does to produce rotation. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule**: This rule is used to find the direction of the **force** acting on a **current-carrying conductor** in a **magnetic field**. If the **forefinger** represents the **magnetic field** and the **middle finger** represents the **current**, then the **thumb** points in the direction of the **motion** or **force**.
 
• **Lorentz Force**: The fundamental physics behind this is the **Lorentz force law**, which states that a point charge moving in a magnetic field experiences a force. For a wire of **length L** carrying **current I** in a **magnetic field B**, the force **F** is calculated as **F = BIL sin(theta)**.
 
• **Applications of Electric Motors**: These are used in a wide variety of daily appliances including **water pumps**, **electric fans**, **washing machines**, **mixers**, **refrigerators**, and **electric cars**.
 
• **Commutator**: In a **DC motor**, a device called a **split-ring commutator** is used to reverse the direction of **current** every half rotation, ensuring the **torque** remains in the same direction and the motor continues to spin.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Armature**: The **soft iron core** on which the coil is wound is called an **armature**. This enhances the **power** of the motor by increasing the **magnetic flux**.
 
• **Magnetic Field Sources**: Commercial motors use an **electromagnet** instead of a **permanent magnet** to create a much stronger **magnetic field**, allowing the motor to perform heavy-duty work.
 
• **Energy Transformation**: While a **motor** converts **electrical to mechanical energy**, an **electric generator** works on the reverse principle (**Electromagnetic Induction**) to convert **mechanical to electrical energy**.
 
• **Efficiency**: Modern electric motors can be highly efficient, often converting over **90 percent** of **electrical energy** into **useful mechanical work**, far surpassing internal combustion engines.

questions.question: Which of the following sound frequencies is inaudible to humans?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**25,000 Hz**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The human ear is sensitive to sound waves within a specific frequency range, typically defined as **20 Hz to 20,000 Hz** (or **20 kHz**).
 
• Any sound frequency that falls outside this range is generally considered **inaudible** to the average human being.
 
• **25,000 Hz** is greater than the upper limit of **20,000 Hz**, making it **inaudible** to humans. ***Hence, option 2 is correct.***
 
• **5000 Hz** falls comfortably within the audible range. ***Hence, option 1 is audible and incorrect.***
 
• **50 Hz** is at the lower end of the audible spectrum but is still perceivable by the human ear. ***Hence, option 3 is audible and incorrect.***
 
• **2000 Hz** is within the range where human hearing is most sensitive, particularly for speech. ***Hence, option 4 is audible and incorrect.***
 
• The unit of frequency is the **Hertz (Hz)**, named after the German physicist **Heinrich Rudolf Hertz**, which represents **one cycle per second**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Classification of Sound based on Frequency:**
 
 
• **Infrasonic Sound:** These are sounds with frequencies lower than **20 Hz**. They are produced by large sources like **earthquakes**, **volcanic eruptions**, and **ocean waves**. Animals like **elephants** and **whales** can communicate using infrasound over long distances.
 
• **Audible Sound:** The standard range for humans is **20 Hz to 20,000 Hz**. Sensitivity varies with **age** and **exposure** to loud noises; children can often hear slightly higher frequencies than adults.
 
• **Ultrasonic Sound (Ultrasound):** These are sounds with frequencies higher than **20,000 Hz**. While humans cannot hear them, animals such as **bats**, **dogs**, and **dolphins** can perceive and utilize these frequencies.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Ultrasound:**
 
 
• **Medical Imaging:** Used in **ultrasonography** (sonogram) to visualize internal organs and monitor fetal development during pregnancy.
 
• **SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging):** Used by ships and submarines to detect underwater objects or measure the **depth of the sea**.
 
• **Industrial Cleaning:** High-frequency waves are used to clean parts located in hard-to-reach places, such as **spiral tubes** and **electronic components**.
 
 
 
• **Physics of Sound:**
 
 
• Sound is a **mechanical longitudinal wave** that requires a **medium** (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel. It cannot travel through a **vacuum**.
 
• The **pitch** of a sound is directly related to its **frequency**; higher frequency results in a higher pitch (shrill sound), while lower frequency results in a lower pitch (bass sound).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Hearing Loss and Age:** As humans age, a condition known as **presbycusis** often occurs, where the ability to hear high-frequency sounds (near **15,000 Hz - 20,000 Hz**) diminishes first.
 
• **Dogs and Whistles:** Special whistles known as **Galton's whistles** produce sounds in the **ultrasonic range** (above **20,000 Hz**). Dogs can hear these signals, but they remain silent to human observers.
 
• **Speed of Sound:** The speed of sound is approximately **343 meters per second** in dry air at **20°C**. It travels fastest in **solids** and slowest in **gases**.
 
• **Intensity vs. Frequency:** It is important to distinguish between **frequency** (pitch, measured in **Hz**) and **intensity/loudness** (measured in **Decibels or dB**). A frequency of **25,000 Hz** is inaudible regardless of how "loud" (intense) it is played.

questions.question: What happens to the uterine lining in human females if the egg is not fertilized?

options.text: It thickens further for another week.
It breaks down and is discharged as blood and mucus.
It remains intact for the next cycle.
It is reabsorbed into the body.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It breaks down and is discharged as blood and mucus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The **uterus** (womb) prepares itself every month to receive a **fertilized egg**. To provide a nourishing environment for a potential **embryo**, the inner lining of the uterus, known as the **endometrium**, becomes **thick and spongy**, rich with blood vessels.
 
• If **fertilization** by a **sperm** does not occur, the **ovum** (egg) survives for about **one day**. Since the egg is not fertilized, the thick lining of the uterus is no longer required for **implantation** or **pregnancy**.
 
• As the levels of hormones like **progesterone** and **estrogen** drop, the **uterine lining** begins to **break down** slowly.
 
• This broken-down lining, along with the unfertilized egg and blood, is **discharged** from the body through the **vagina**. This process is called **menstruation**.

questions.question: In terms of chromosome contribution, which of the following is correct?

options.text: Mother always contributes X, father contributes X or Y
Both parents contribute either X or Y
Mother can contribute X or Y

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mother always contributes X, father contributes X or Y**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In humans, the **sex of a child** is determined by the types of **chromosomes** inherited from the parents. Human cells contain **23 pairs** of chromosomes, out of which **22 pairs** are **autosomes** and **one pair** is the **sex chromosome**.
 
• Females have a **homogametic** sex chromosome makeup, meaning they possess two identical **X chromosomes (XX)**. During the process of **meiosis** and **gamete formation**, every egg produced by a female will carry an **X chromosome**. ***Hence, the statement that the mother always contributes an X chromosome is correct.***
 
• Males have a **heterogametic** sex chromosome makeup, consisting of one **X chromosome** and one **Y chromosome (XY)**. Consequently, **50%** of the sperms produced by a male carry the **X chromosome**, while the other **50%** carry the **Y chromosome**. ***Hence, the statement that the father contributes X or Y is correct.***
 
• If a sperm carrying an **X chromosome** fertilizes an egg (which always has an X), the resulting zygote will be **XX**, leading to a **female child**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect as the father can also contribute a Y chromosome.***
 
• If a sperm carrying a **Y chromosome** fertilizes an egg, the resulting zygote will be **XY**, leading to a **male child**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect because the mother cannot contribute a Y chromosome.***
 
• The genetic probability for the birth of a boy or a girl is **50:50**, and it depends entirely on the **chromosome** contributed by the **father's sperm**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect because the mother cannot contribute "either" X or Y.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sex Determination Systems**:
 
 
• While humans use the **XY system**, other organisms have different mechanisms. In **birds**, the sex determination follows a **ZW system** where the **female is heterogametic (ZW)** and the **male is homogametic (ZZ)**.
 
• In certain insects like **grasshoppers**, an **XO system** is present, where females have **XX** and males have only one **X chromosome (XO)**.
 
 
 
• **The Y Chromosome and SRY Gene**:
 
 
• The **Y chromosome** is significantly smaller than the **X chromosome**. It contains the **SRY gene (Sex-determining Region Y)**, which is responsible for triggering the development of **male characteristics** in an embryo.
 
• In the absence of a functional **SRY gene**, the embryo will typically develop **female** reproductive structures.
 
 
 
• **Chromosomal Abnormalities**:
 
 
• Errors during **cell division** can lead to conditions like **Turner Syndrome (45, XO)**, where an individual has only one X chromosome, or **Klinefelter Syndrome (47, XXY)**, where a male has an extra X chromosome.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **History**: The **X chromosome** was first identified by **Hermann Henking** in **1891** during his study of insects, though he initially called it the "**X-body**."
 
• **Inheritance**: Since a male (XY) always receives his **Y chromosome** from his **father**, the Y chromosome can be used to trace **patrilineal ancestry**. Similarly, because **mitochondrial DNA** is inherited only from the **mother**, it is used for **matrilineal tracing**.
 
• **Function of X Chromosome**: Unlike the Y chromosome, the **X chromosome** contains over **900 genes**, many of which are essential for **biological functions** unrelated to sex, such as **blood clotting** and **color vision**.
</ul

questions.question: Materials that have NOT been broken down by the action of bacteria or saprophytes, but somehow degraded by physical processes, are called:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Non-biodegradable**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Non-biodegradable** materials are substances that cannot be decomposed, dissolved, or broken down by natural biological agents such as **bacteria**, **fungi**, or **saprophytes**.

• While these materials resist biological decay, they are subject to **physical processes** such as **photodegradation** (breakdown by **UV radiation** from the sun), **thermal degradation**, and **mechanical weathering** caused by wind or water.

• These substances are typically **synthetic** or man-made, featuring strong chemical bonds that natural **enzymes** cannot penetrate or metabolize.

• Because they are not part of the natural **nutrient cycle**, they persist in the **environment** for extremely long periods, ranging from **decades** to **thousands of years**.

• Common examples of such materials include **plastics**, **polythene bags**, **glass**, **metal scraps**, **synthetic fibers** like nylon, and certain **pesticides** like **DDT**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Biodegradable Materials:**

• These are organic substances that can be easily broken down into simpler compounds like **carbon dioxide**, **water**, and **methane** by the action of **microorganisms**.

• Examples include **food waste**, **paper**, **wood**, **leaves**, and **animal waste**. These materials are **eco-friendly** as they return nutrients to the soil.

• **Saprophytes:**

• These are organisms, including certain **bacteria** and **fungi**, that obtain their nutrition from **dead and decaying** organic matter.

• They play a critical role as **decomposers** in the **ecosystem**, but they lack the capacity to process **non-biodegradable** waste due to the absence of specific **catalytic enzymes**.

• **Physical Degradation:**

• This refers to the **fragmentation** of materials into smaller pieces without changing their chemical nature significantly.

• In the case of plastics, physical processes lead to the formation of **microplastics** (particles smaller than **5mm**), which pose a severe threat to **marine life** and enter the **human food chain**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Biomagnification:** Non-biodegradable pollutants like **mercury** and **DDT** do not decompose and instead accumulate in the bodies of organisms. Their concentration increases at each successive **trophic level** of the **food chain**.

• **Environmental Persistence:** A simple **plastic bottle** can take up to **450 years** to fragment through physical processes, while **glass** may take over **1 million years** to break down, highlighting the permanence of **non-biodegradable** waste.

• **Waste Management:** Since biological methods fail, the management of these materials relies on the **3Rs**: **Reduce**, **Reuse**, and **Recycle**. Specialized industrial processes like **pyrolysis** or **incineration** are sometimes used to manage **synthetic polymers**.

• **Impact on Soil:** The accumulation of **non-biodegradable** waste reduces **soil porosity** and interferes with the **nitrogen-fixing** capability of soil **bacteria**, eventually leading to **land degradation**.
</ul

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the characteristics of compounds and select the correct option.

Statement 1: Elements react to form new compounds.
Statement 2: Each new substance formed is of variable composition.
Statement 3: The constituents can be separated only by chemical or electrochemical reactions.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only statements 1 and 3 are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1**: When two or more **elements** undergo a **chemical reaction**, they combine to form a new substance known as a **compound**. This process involves the breaking of old bonds and the formation of new **chemical bonds**, resulting in a product that has entirely different physical and chemical properties from its constituents. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 2**: A **compound** is characterized by a **fixed composition** of its constituent elements by **mass**. Unlike **mixtures**, which can have **variable composition** (meaning the components can be present in any ratio), the elements in a compound are always present in **definite proportions**. For instance, **pure water** will always contain **Hydrogen** and **Oxygen** in a **mass ratio of 1:8**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Statement 3**: The constituents of a **compound** are chemically unified and cannot be separated by simple **physical methods** such as **filtration**, **evaporation**, **distillation**, or **magnetic separation**. Separation of these elements requires the application of energy through **chemical reactions** or **electrochemical reactions**, such as the process of **electrolysis** to separate water into hydrogen and oxygen. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• Consequently, out of the three given statements, only the **first** and the **third** accurately describe the characteristics of a **chemical compound**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Definition of a Compound**: A **compound** is a **pure substance** made up of two or more **elements** chemically combined in a **fixed ratio**. Examples include **Sodium Chloride (NaCl)**, **Methane (CH4)**, and **Carbon Dioxide (CO2)**. A compound is always **homogeneous** in nature, meaning its properties are uniform throughout the sample.
 
• **Properties of Compounds**: The properties of a **compound** are distinctly different from the properties of the **elements** that form it. For example, **Sodium (Na)** is a highly reactive metal and **Chlorine (Cl)** is a poisonous gas, but their compound **Sodium Chloride (Table Salt)** is an edible solid essential for life. Furthermore, compounds have sharp and fixed **melting points** and **boiling points**.
 
• **Comparison with Mixtures**: **Mixtures** are formed by the physical blending of two or more substances where no **chemical reaction** takes place. In a **mixture**, the components retain their original properties and can be separated by **physical means**. Mixtures do not have a fixed **chemical formula** or a fixed **melting point**.
 
• **The Law of Definite Proportions**: Also known as **Proust's Law**, it was formulated by the French chemist **Joseph Proust** in **1799**. It states that a given chemical **compound** always contains its component **elements** in a fixed **ratio** (by **mass**) and does not depend on its source or method of preparation. This is a fundamental law in **stoichiometry**.
 
• **Energy Changes**: The formation of a **compound** is usually accompanied by a significant **energy change** in the form of **heat**, **light**, or **sound** (either **exothermic** or **endothermic** reactions), whereas the formation of a **mixture** involves little to no energy change.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Types of Compounds**: Compounds can be classified into **organic compounds** (containing **carbon-hydrogen bonds**) and **inorganic compounds**. They can also be classified based on the type of bonding, such as **ionic compounds** (held by electrostatic forces) and **covalent compounds** (formed by sharing electrons).
 
• **Electrolysis**: This is a common **electrochemical reaction** used to decompose **compounds**. For example, during the **electrolysis of water**, **electric current** is passed through acidified water to yield **Hydrogen gas** at the **cathode** and **Oxygen gas** at the **anode**.
 
• **Valency**: The formation of a **compound** depends on the **valency** or combining capacity of the **elements** involved. The fixed composition of a compound is a direct result of the specific number of **atoms** of each element required to satisfy their **valence shells** and reach a stable **electronic configuration**.
</ul

questions.question: ___ generally has long, unstable carbon chains.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vegetable oil**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Vegetable oil** is primarily composed of **triglycerides**, which are esters derived from **glycerol** and three **fatty acids**. These fatty acids consist of **long carbon chains** typically ranging from **12 to 22 carbon atoms** in length.
 
• The "unstable" nature mentioned in the question refers to the **unsaturated** characteristic of most vegetable oils. **Unsaturated fatty acids** contain one or more **double bonds** within their carbon chains, which makes them chemically more reactive than **saturated fats**.
 
• These **double bonds** are sites where **oxidation** can occur, leading to the oil becoming **rancid** when exposed to air and light. This chemical reactivity is why they are considered "unstable" compared to shorter or fully saturated carbon structures.
 
• In contrast, **Glucose** has a relatively short and highly stable **six-carbon chain** (often forming a ring structure), while **Water** and **Table salt** are inorganic compounds that do not contain carbon chains at all.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structure of Vegetable Oils:**
 
 
• Vegetable oils like **sunflower oil**, **mustard oil**, and **groundnut oil** are liquids at **room temperature** because the "kinks" created by **double bonds** in their **unsaturated carbon chains** prevent the molecules from packing closely together.
 
• The process of **hydrogenation** is often used in the food industry to convert these unstable liquid oils into **saturated solid fats** (like **vanaspati ghee**) by adding hydrogen across the double bonds in the presence of a **Nickel catalyst**.
 
 
 
• **Glucose (C6H12O6):**
 
 
• It is a **monosaccharide** and serves as the primary **energy source** for living organisms.
 
• It contains only **6 carbon atoms**, which is much shorter than the chains found in oils. Its structure is very stable under normal physiological conditions.
 
 
 
• **Water (H2O):**
 
 
• Known as the **universal solvent**, water is an **inorganic** polar covalent compound.
 
• It contains **zero carbon atoms** and therefore does not possess carbon chains.
 
 
 
• **Table Salt (NaCl):**
 
 
• Scientifically known as **Sodium Chloride**, it is an **ionic compound** formed by the attraction between sodium cations and chloride anions.
 
• It forms a **crystalline lattice** structure and, like water, contains **no carbon**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Health Implications:** **Unsaturated vegetable oils** are generally considered healthier for the **human heart** compared to saturated fats, as they help maintain better **cholesterol levels**, despite being chemically less stable.
 
• **Carbon Chain Length:** In organic chemistry, the **stability** of a molecule is often dictated by the types of **chemical bonds** (single vs. double vs. triple) rather than just the length. However, in the context of nutrition and lipids, **long unsaturated chains** are the hallmark of liquid oils.
 
• **Reactivity:** The presence of multiple **double bonds** makes an oil **polyunsaturated**. These are the most "unstable" and prone to **polymerization** and **oxidation** when heated to high temperatures (the **smoke point**).
</ul

questions.question: When two bodies interact, the action and reaction forces _________.

options.text: produce the same effect on both bodies

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**act on different bodies**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Newton's Third Law of Motion** states that whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object exerts an equal and opposite force on the first. This is often summarized as "to every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction."
 
• The action and reaction forces are always equal in **magnitude** but opposite in **direction**. They represent a mutual interaction between two entities.
 
• A fundamental characteristic of these forces is that they **act on different bodies**. For instance, if Body A exerts a force on Body B (action), Body B exerts a force on Body A (reaction). Because they are applied to different objects, they do not cancel each other out. ***Hence, the statement in option 4 is correct.***
 
• The forces do not produce the **same effect** on both bodies if their **masses** are different. According to **Newton's Second Law** (F = ma), the body with smaller mass will experience a greater **acceleration** compared to the body with larger mass. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• Action and reaction forces never act in the **same direction**; they are always oriented **180 degrees** apart. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• If action and reaction were to **act on the same body**, the **net force** would always be **zero**, making acceleration or motion impossible for any object under interaction. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Newton's Laws of Motion**: These three physical laws were first compiled by **Sir Isaac Newton** in his work **Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica**, published in **1687**. They form the foundation of **classical mechanics**.
 
• **First Law (Law of Inertia)**: An object remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external **force**.
 
• **Second Law**: The rate of change of **momentum** of an object is proportional to the applied **force** and takes place in the direction of the force. It is mathematically expressed as **F = ma**.
 
• **Examples of the Third Law**:
 
 
• **Walking**: When a person walks, they push the ground backward with their feet (action), and the ground pushes the person forward with an equal force (reaction).
 
• **Recoil of a Gun**: When a bullet is fired from a **gun**, the gun exerts a forward force on the bullet. The bullet exerts an equal and opposite backward force on the gun, causing it to **recoil**.
 
• **Rocket Propulsion**: A **rocket** accelerates by expelling gas backward at high velocity. The reacting force of the gas pushes the rocket forward in the **vacuum of space**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Simultaneity**: There is no time lag between action and reaction. They occur **simultaneously**. One is not the "cause" of the other in a chronological sense; they are two sides of a single interaction.
 
• **Nature of Forces**: Both the action and reaction forces are of the **same nature**. For example, if the action is a **gravitational force**, the reaction is also a gravitational force. If the action is a **contact force** (like friction or normal force), the reaction is also a contact force.
 
• **Vector Quantity**: Force is a **vector quantity**, meaning it has both **magnitude** and **direction**. The sum of the action-reaction vector pair across the system is zero, which is a basis for the **Law of Conservation of Momentum**.

questions.question: The Indian hockey legend PR Sreejesh was recognized with what specific prestigious honour by President Droupadi Murmu on 28 April 2025, at Rashtrapati Bhavan?

__
 
• The legendary Indian hockey goalkeeper **PR Sreejesh** was conferred with the **Padma Bhushan**, India's **third-highest civilian award**, by **President Droupadi Murmu**.
 
• The ceremony took place at the **Rashtrapati Bhavan** on **28 April 2025**, recognizing his "distinguished service of high order" to the nation in the field of **Sports**.
 
• **PR Sreejesh** is widely regarded as one of the greatest goalkeepers in the history of field hockey, often referred to as "**The Wall of India**" for his exceptional defensive skills.
 
• The award acknowledges his immense contribution to the resurgence of **Indian Hockey** on the global stage, particularly his role in securing consecutive **Olympic medals**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Padma Bhushan.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• He played a pivotal role in India winning the **Bronze Medal** at the **Tokyo 2020 Olympics**, ending a **41-year** Olympic medal drought for Indian hockey.
